title: The ode: date, cancelled opening, Burton
short: Written in spring 1819 and published in 1820; Keats cancelled a grotesque first stanza, so the poem now begins with an emphatic refusal.
body: The ode belongs to the group of odes Keats wrote in spring 1819 and was printed in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems (1820). The manuscript shows a cancelled opening stanza, beginning 'Though you should build a bark of dead men's bones', which parodied gothic quests for melancholy; its removal leaves the poem starting abruptly with a doubled 'No'. Keats owned and annotated Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), which supplied much traditional lore about melancholy. The poem's argument is that true melancholy is found not in images of death but in the intense experience of beauty and joy, which carry their own transience.

title: Lethe
short: The river of forgetfulness in the classical underworld; drinking its water wipes out memory.
body: In Greek and Roman myth Lethe (Greek 'forgetfulness') is a river of Hades; the souls of the dead drink from it to forget their former lives, as in Virgil, Aeneid 6, where souls waiting to be reborn drink the waters of 'long oblivion'. The speaker forbids the melancholic to seek oblivion, because forgetfulness would deaden the feeling melancholy depends on. Keats had used Lethe in the opening of the 'Ode to a Nightingale' ('Lethe-wards had sunk'), written in the same spring.

title: Wolf's-bane
short: Aconite, a deadly poisonous plant; its 'wine' is a poison distilled from its root.
body: Wolf's-bane is aconite or monkshood (Aconitum), whose roots are highly toxic; the name comes from its use in poisoning wolves. In Ovid (Metamorphoses 7) aconite springs from the foam of Cerberus' jaws, and Medea uses it to poison Theseus, so it carries classical associations with the underworld. 'Tight-rooted' stresses how firmly the plant grips the ground, picturing a deliberate and laborious gathering of poison. The poisonous 'wine' anticipates the grape imagery of ll. 4 and 28.

title: nightshade, ruby grape of Proserpine
short: Deadly nightshade's red berry is pictured as the grape of Proserpine, queen of the underworld.
body: Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna) bears poisonous berries; Keats calls it the 'ruby grape' of Proserpine (Greek Persephone), who was carried off by Pluto to be queen of the underworld and was bound there because she ate pomegranate seeds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5). The metaphor makes the poison a seductive fruit offered by death's queen; to be 'kiss'd' on the forehead by it is to be drugged towards death. Belladonna's name ('beautiful lady') and its botanical genus named after the Fate Atropos may also lie behind the image of a deadly beauty. The grape returns transformed as 'Joy's grape' in l. 28.

title: rosary of yew-berries
short: Do not make a string of prayer beads out of poisonous yew berries, the fruit of the churchyard tree.
body: A rosary is a string of beads used to count prayers, especially in Catholic devotion. The yew, long planted in churchyards, is an emblem of death and mourning, and its seeds and foliage are poisonous. A rosary of yew-berries would turn melancholy into a morbid religious ritual, praying on death. Keats's catalogue rejects this conventional 'graveyard' apparatus of eighteenth-century melancholy poetry (Young, Blair, Gray's 'Elegy').

title: the beetle, nor the death-moth
short: Creatures of death-lore: probably the scarab or death-watch beetle, and the death's-head hawk-moth with its skull-like marking.
body: The 'death-moth' is the death's-head hawk-moth, whose thorax bears a mark like a human skull and which was regarded as an omen of death. The beetle has been read as the Egyptian scarab, placed in tombs as a symbol of the soul's rebirth, or as the death-watch beetle, whose ticking in old timbers was supposed to foretell a death. Either way, these insects are offered as false emblems of the soul; see the note on 'Psyche'.

title: mournful Psyche
short: Psyche is Greek for both 'soul' and 'butterfly'; the melancholic should not take a death-insect as the emblem of the soul.
body: In Greek, psyche means breath, soul and also butterfly, and ancient art represented the soul as a butterfly leaving the body. Psyche is also the heroine of the myth in Apuleius' Golden Ass, loved by Cupid and finally made immortal; Keats had just written his 'Ode to Psyche' (April 1819). The line warns against letting a beetle or a death's-head moth stand in for one's soul: to do so would be to make death the image of the self.

title: the downy owl
short: The owl, a traditional bird of night and ill omen, should not be the melancholic's companion.
body: The owl's nocturnal cry was a conventional omen of death (compare Macbeth 2.2) and it had become a stock prop of melancholy verse, as in Gray's 'Elegy' ('the moping owl'). 'Downy' (soft-feathered) adds a sleepy softness that matches the warning that follows: these comforts lull rather than sharpen sorrow. 'A partner in your sorrow's mysteries' turns melancholy into a secret religious cult, continuing the rosary image.

title: For shade to shade will come too drowsily
short: Darkness added to darkness dulls the mind; the soul's anguish must be kept awake, not drugged.
body: This is the reason for all the prohibitions. 'Shade to shade' may mean the gloom of these death-images joining the gloom of the melancholic mind, or the soul (a 'shade' in classical idiom) coming to the realm of shades, death. Either way the result is drowsiness, which would 'drown' the 'wakeful anguish' that the speaker values. The paradox, that anguish should be preserved because it is a form of intense consciousness, governs the whole ode. Vendler stresses the poem's preference for heightened, not numbed, sensation.

title: the melancholy fit
short: A sudden attack of melancholy, in the older medical sense of a bout of a humoral disorder.
body: In humoral medicine melancholy was caused by an excess of black bile (Greek melaina chole), and a 'fit' was a sudden onset or paroxysm of the condition. Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, which Keats read closely, treats melancholy both as a disease and as a disposition. Keats imagines the fit descending 'Sudden from heaven', like weather, not something one seeks out with poisons and charms.

title: weeping cloud / April shroud
short: Melancholy comes like a spring shower, which both nourishes the flowers and veils the hill like a burial cloth.
body: The simile is double-edged. The 'weeping cloud' fosters the drooping flowers, so sorrow is fertile, part of the cycle of growth; yet it also hides the green hill in a 'shroud', the cloth in which the dead are wrapped. April showers are brief and life-giving, so the image suggests that melancholy is natural and seasonal rather than morbid. The 'droop-headed' flowers are both refreshed and bowed by the rain.

title: glut thy sorrow on a morning rose
short: Feast your sorrow to the full on transient beauty: the rose that will fade by evening.
body: 'Glut' means to feed to excess, to gorge, and introduces the ode's language of eating and tasting. The objects on which sorrow should feast are beautiful and short-lived: a morning rose, a rainbow in the spray of a breaking wave, a full peony. The advice is to intensify melancholy by attending fully to beauty in the knowledge that it will vanish. Keats's sensuous excess here risks, and embraces, a kind of indulgence.

title: the rainbow of the salt sand-wave
short: The momentary rainbow that shows in the spray of a wave breaking on sand.
body: A compound image of extreme transience: the colours appear in the spray only as the wave breaks, and vanish at once. 'Sand-wave' suggests a wave churned with sand at the shoreline. The rainbow, a traditional sign of promise and beauty (Genesis 9:13), is here valued precisely for its brevity. 'Salt' adds a sharp, tasting sensation, continuing the ode's appeal to the palate, and the sea setting recalls the shores and waters of Keats's other 1819 poems. Each object in the series is a beauty that exists only in the moment of perception.

title: the wealth of globed peonies
short: The full, rounded blooms of the peony, abundant and on the point of falling.
body: Peonies form heavy spherical flower-heads ('globed') that drop their petals soon after full bloom. 'Wealth' stresses their lavish fullness. The roundness anticipates the bursting grape of l. 28, and some critics have read sensual, even sexual suggestion into the ode's imagery of full, ripe forms. The run of three objects (rose, rainbow, peonies) moves from a single flower to a light-effect to massed abundance.

title: if thy mistress some rich anger shows
short: If the beloved flares up in anger, treat even that as a rich spectacle of beauty.
body: The ode turns from nature to a woman. Her anger is 'rich' because it heightens her beauty and intensity; the lover is told to 'Emprison her soft hand' (hold it captive) and let her 'rave'. Modern readers often find the lines troubling, since the woman becomes an object of aesthetic consumption whose feelings matter only as spectacle. Others read the stanza as dramatizing the lover's absorption rather than endorsing it.

title: feed deep, deep upon her peerless eyes
short: Gaze intensely into her matchless eyes, as if eating; the repetition marks absorption.
body: The verb 'feed' continues 'glut' and anticipates the tasting of Joy's grape. The doubled 'deep, deep' slows the line and imitates prolonged absorption. 'Peerless' (without equal) echoes Renaissance love poetry. The stanza ends in a moment of total, almost devouring attention, which the third stanza will reveal as itself the dwelling place of Melancholy. The eyes are the traditional seat of the beloved's power in Petrarchan verse, but Keats makes the lover's gaze a kind of nourishment, consistent with his habit of rendering every sense through taste.

title: She dwells with Beauty
short: 'She' most naturally refers to the mistress, but many readers take it as Melancholy herself; the ambiguity is productive.
body: Grammatically 'She' follows the mistress of stanza 2, who lives with a beauty that must die. But the stanza goes on to describe Melancholy's shrine, and many editors and critics read 'She' as Melancholy, personified as a goddess who lives alongside Beauty, Joy and Pleasure. Many readers take the slippage to be deliberate: the beloved and melancholy become indistinguishable, since to love mortal beauty is already to dwell with sadness. The personified Joy, 'Bidding adieu' with hand at lips, and 'aching Pleasure' are allegorical figures in a classical or Spenserian manner.

title: Joy, whose hand is ever at his lips / Bidding adieu
short: Joy is pictured always blowing a farewell kiss: it begins to leave the moment it arrives.
body: The gesture is a kiss of farewell. The allegory compresses a philosophical point, that joy is inherently fleeting, into a single frozen pose, much like the figures on the Grecian urn. 'Aching Pleasure' in the next line combines pain and delight; Pleasure turns 'to poison' even as the bee sips the nectar, recalling the poisons of stanza 1, now found inside delight itself.

title: while the bee-mouth sips
short: Pleasure turns to poison in the very act of tasting, as the bee drinks nectar.
body: The compound 'bee-mouth' is a striking Keatsian coinage. The bee was a traditional image of gathering sweetness, but here the sweetness becomes poison as it is consumed. The ancient belief in poisonous honey (the 'mad honey' of the Black Sea region) may lie behind the idea; the main point is the simultaneity of pleasure and its loss. The line prepares for the climactic tasting of 'Joy's grape'.

title: Veil'd Melancholy has her sovran shrine
short: Melancholy is a veiled goddess whose supreme shrine stands inside the temple of Delight itself.
body: 'Sovran' is an archaic, Miltonic spelling of 'sovereign', meaning supreme. The architectural allegory places the goddess Melancholy within the temple of Delight: sorrow is not opposed to joy but enshrined at its centre. She is 'Veil'd', hidden like a mystery-cult deity, visible only to the initiated (continuing 'sorrow's mysteries' from stanza 1). Burton describes melancholy as close neighbour to joy, and Keats's image gives this commonplace a religious, ritual form.

title: burst Joy's grape against his palate fine
short: Only a person of intense, refined sensibility, who crushes joy fully on the tongue, can see Melancholy.
body: The initiate is one 'whose strenuous tongue / Can burst Joy's grape against his palate fine'. The grape recalls Proserpine's poisonous berry in stanza 1, now become the fruit of joy. 'Strenuous' implies effort and vigour; 'palate fine' a discriminating taste, both literal and aesthetic. The image says that only maximum intensity of pleasure reveals its inseparable sadness. The phrase 'burst Joy's grape' has attracted detailed critical analysis (Daniel Brass is cited in the Wikipedia survey of the poem).

title: among her cloudy trophies hung
short: The soul becomes one of Melancholy's trophies, hung in her temple like spoils dedicated by a victor.
body: In Greek and Roman practice, victors hung captured arms and spoils (trophies) in temples as offerings to a deity. The soul that has tasted joy fully becomes one of Melancholy's spoils, defeated and displayed. 'Cloudy' recalls the 'weeping cloud' of stanza 2 and suggests the trophies are shadowy, insubstantial. The ending is ambiguous: to be hung among her trophies is to be conquered, yet also to be consecrated in her shrine, the privilege of those capable of the deepest feeling.

title: The ode stanza
short: Three ten-line pentameter stanzas, each a quatrain followed by a sestet, a form Keats developed from the sonnet for the 1819 odes.
body: Keats built the stanza of the 1819 odes out of his experience with the sonnet: an opening Shakespearean quatrain (abab) followed by a Petrarchan-style sestet. In this ode stanzas 1 and 2 rhyme ababcdecde; stanza 3 varies the sestet to cdedce. Most lines are iambic pentameter, though the lines are indented to mark the rhyme pattern, as the archive text preserves. The compact form suits the poem's argument, which moves from prohibition (st. 1) to prescription (st. 2) to allegorical revelation (st. 3).
